analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share repair information and diagnostic tools with independent repair shops and owners.
analysis.headline: A right-to-repair bill with 108 bipartisan sponsors, including the committee chairman himself, never got a House floor vote, dying in committee after a narrow 14-13 subcommittee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Modern cars are run by computers, and automakers were restricting access to the diagnostic codes, service information, and tools needed to fix them. The bill would have required manufacturers to give car owners and independent repair shops the same repair information and tools their franchised dealerships get, with the Federal Trade Commission writing the rules and enforcing violations. Trade secrets and emissions-related systems were protected from the mandate.
analysis.who_benefits: Car owners, who would be able to get their vehicles fixed at any shop of their choosing instead of being pushed back to dealership service departments, likely at lower prices through competition. Independent repair shops and the automotive aftermarket — an industry the bill's own findings say employs over 5 million workers in over 495,000 businesses and generates $200 billion in annual sales — would gain access to the information and tools they need to compete [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to promptly provide owners or their chosen repair facility the information necessary to diagnose, service, or repair a vehicle, and to make non-emission-related service, training, and diagnostic information available on the same basis to independent shops as to franchised dealerships [S2][S3].

Requires that the same diagnostic tools and capabilities given to dealerships be made available for purchase by owners and independent shops, so owners would not need to return to a dealership for repairs [S3].

The bill's findings state that restricted access to repair information limits consumer choice, impedes competition, and increases repair costs, and that access codes often prevent timely, affordable repairs [S3].
Makes noncompliance an unfair or deceptive practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act, enforceable by the FTC, so the disclosure requirement has teeth [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would have to build and maintain disclosure systems for repair information and tools they previously restricted, and franchised dealership service departments, which would face more competition for repair work. Some compliance costs could ultimately be reflected in vehicle prices.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers argued the mandate forces disclosure of valuable technical information; the bill responds by carving out trade secrets and information related exclusively to part design and manufacture, but the boundary would be tested in practice [S3].
Compliance is not free: automakers would bear the cost of providing information, tools, and training to any shop, and some of that cost may be passed to car buyers [S3].

The FTC must write the rules without interfering with EPA authority over emissions diagnostics, a jurisdictional split that could leave gaps in coverage for emissions-related repair information [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to owners — competitive repair pricing and the ability to fix safety-critical systems anywhere — are broad and ongoing, while the main costs fall on a concentrated set of manufacturers whose information-sharing programs already existed for their own dealer networks. The strongest honest objection is that defining the trade-secret carve-out and coordinating with EPA emissions rules would take careful regulation, but the bill leaves enforcement to the FTC with established procedures.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee its whole life: a subcommittee heard testimony, debated it, and forwarded it to the full committee by just 14-13, but the full committee never voted and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced May 3, 2005 by Rep. Joe Barton, then chairman of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, with Reps. Towns and Issa, and referred to the committee he chaired [S1][S3][S5].
It gathered 107 cosponsors — 67 Democrats, 39 Republicans, and 1 Independent — a large bipartisan show of support [S4].
The bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, which held a hearing on May 17, 2006 and a mark-up session on May 25, 2006 [S1][S5].
On May 25, 2006 the subcommittee forwarded an amended bill to the full committee by a vote of only 14-13 [S1][S5].
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never took action, and the bill never reached the House floor before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and franchised dealership service departments, who kept restricting repair information and faced no disclosure mandate. Car owners and independent shops kept bearing the cost of restricted access.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 67 Democrats, 39 Republicans, and 1 Independent cosponsored, and the Republican committee chairman sponsored it — while the subcommittee advanced it by the narrowest margin, 14-13.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to share diagnostic codes, service information, and tools with independent shops and owners, ending an information advantage they had used to steer repairs to their own dealer networks [S3]. Their interest in keeping that information restricted runs against owners' ability to repair their vehicles affordably.
Dealerships' service operations would lose the captive-repair advantage of exclusive access to manufacturer diagnostic tools and information, facing price competition from independent shops [S3].

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and the automotive aftermarket
industries.note: The bill would give them the same repair information and tools as franchised dealerships. The aftermarket industry, which the bill's findings say employs over 5 million workers across 495,000 businesses, would be able to compete fully for owners' repair business [S3].

A mandate that manufacturers sell diagnostic tools through reasonable business means to any shop or owner would expand the market for repair equipment, though FTC disclosure rules would shape the terms [S3].
